facts.title: Born from boiled urine
facts.text: Phosphorus was the first element discovered with a known discoverer: the German alchemist Hennig Brand isolated it in Hamburg around 1669 while boiling down vast quantities of urine in search of gold. The glowing white substance he produced was the first new element found since antiquity. Brand kept his method secret for years, but the recipe eventually spread across Europe.

facts.title: Named for the morning star
facts.text: The name phosphorus comes from the Ancient Greek 'phosphoros', meaning 'light-bearer' or 'bringer of light'. It was originally a name for the planet Venus when it appears as the morning star. The element earned it because white phosphorus glows faintly in the dark, a property that fascinated early scientists.

facts.title: It glows by slow burning
facts.text: The eerie green glow of white phosphorus in air is not heat or radioactivity but chemiluminescence: the phosphorus slowly reacts with oxygen, emitting light without much warmth. Ironically, the word 'phosphorescence' was coined from this element, even though the glow is technically chemiluminescence, not true phosphorescence. The effect gave rise to the broader scientific term still used today.

facts.title: Many faces, one element
facts.text: Phosphorus exists in strikingly different allotropes that behave like different substances entirely. White phosphorus is waxy, toxic and ignites in air near 30 degrees Celsius, while red phosphorus is far more stable and is the material struck on the side of a matchbox. Black phosphorus, the most stable form, conducts electricity and forms layered sheets similar to graphite, making it a candidate for future electronics.

facts.title: Half your DNA backbone
facts.text: Phosphorus is one of the six essential elements of life, and it forms the literal backbone of DNA and RNA through phosphate groups linking the sugar molecules. It is also central to ATP, the energy currency that powers nearly every process in your cells. Without phosphorus, there would be no genetic code and no way for living things to store and spend energy.

facts.title: Stored in your bones
facts.text: About 85 percent of the phosphorus in your body is locked into your bones and teeth, combined with calcium as a mineral called hydroxyapatite. An adult human body contains roughly 700 grams of phosphorus in total. This mineral gives skeletons their hardness while also acting as a reserve the body can draw on when blood phosphate runs low.

facts.title: It feeds the world
facts.text: Phosphorus is irreplaceable in agriculture because plants cannot grow without it, and most of the world's supply is mined as phosphate rock for fertilizer. Morocco and Western Sahara together hold the majority of known reserves, giving the region enormous influence over global food production. Because there is no substitute for phosphorus in fertilizer, scientists warn of a future 'peak phosphorus' supply challenge.

facts.title: From matches to safer matches
facts.text: Early friction matches used toxic white phosphorus, and factory workers who inhaled its fumes suffered a horrific bone disease called 'phossy jaw'. The 1906 Bern Convention banned white phosphorus in matches, pushing manufacturers to switch to safer red phosphorus. Today's safety matches keep the red phosphorus on the striking strip, separate from the match head.

facts.title: Forged in dying stars
facts.text: The phosphorus in your body was created inside massive stars and scattered through space when they exploded as supernovae. Astronomers have found that phosphorus is relatively rare in the cosmos compared to other life-essential elements, which raises intriguing questions about where life's phosphorus came from. In 2020 researchers traced phosphorus-bearing molecules from a star-forming region to a comet, hinting that comets may have delivered it to early Earth.

facts.title: A weapon and a medicine
facts.text: Phosphorus chemistry spans extremes: nerve agents and many pesticides are organophosphorus compounds that disrupt the nervous system, while other phosphorus compounds save lives. Bisphosphonate drugs treat osteoporosis by strengthening bone, and radioactive phosphorus-32 has been used to treat certain blood disorders. The same element that can poison can also heal, depending entirely on how its atoms are arranged.
